summary:
Curaçao stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here. It is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, holding full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

In April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed that LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights without delay, and a package of rights requests was delivered to ministers in The Hague. The agreement commits the Kingdom's governments to equal treatment rather than establishing an immediately enforceable right for a visitor.

Curaçao opened an LGBT community centre, the Pink House, in 2010, and the island is presented in regional reporting as one of the more gay-friendly destinations inside the Kingdom.

Public LGBT events have met administrative obstruction. In 2013 a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit condition forced Curaçao's Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel, evidence that event authorisation remains a point of exposure for visibly LGBT gatherings.
tangentialFactors:
Aruba, a separate constituent country of the Kingdom, passed same-sex civil partnerships on 8 September 2016. That is comparator context and does not alter the law a visitor encounters in Curaçao.

Curaçao, Aruba and Sint Maarten are described in regional reporting as drivers of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom, and the three ABC islands (Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao) are profiled together as comparatively gay-friendly within it.

Frank Holtslag of Curaçao Gay Pride cites an IGLTA award in describing Curaçao as the most gay-welcoming destination in the region. This is a promotional claim by a local advocacy figure, not a legal finding, and it sits alongside the 2013 permit obstruction rather than displacing it.
localsOnly:
Curaçao's commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano publicly endorsed equal rights for everyone. That endorsement ran against organised opposition from within her own party: Winifred Raveneau's fierce resistance formed part of the domestic debate over LGBT equality on the island.

Raveneau's opposition had practical effect in 2013, when a last-minute permit set at exceptionally strict conditions obliged the Gay Pride organisers to move the event to a hotel.

The Pink House, opened in 2010, operates as the island's LGBT community centre and is the main organised point of contact for local LGBT residents.
outOfScopeNotes:
Nothing in the source inventory addresses gender-marker or document rules for visitors, passport and visa screening that could expose a trans traveller, bathroom or facilities access, restrictions on gender-affirming healthcare, or hate-crime protection. Those areas are not sourced here and remain unresolved for Curaçao.

Whether the April 2015 Kingdom commitment to equal rights has been carried into binding legislation in Curaçao is not sourced; the inventory records the political agreement and the package of requests submitted in The Hague only.

Whether national Netherlands provisions on legal gender recognition extend to Curaçao, and under which instrument, is not stated in the inventory.
